questions.stem: Rule 11 says the rules in Section II apply to which vessels?
options: All vessels in any condition of visibility
Vessels in sight of one another
Vessels not in sight of one another in restricted visibility
Only power-driven vessels over 20 metres
questions.explanation: Rule 11 limits Section II to vessels in sight of one another. 'Any condition of visibility' describes Section I (Rule 4). Vessels not in sight of one another in or near restricted visibility fall under Rule 19 in Section III. Section II is not limited by vessel type or length.

questions.stem: Which Rules make up Section II of Part B?
options: Rules 4 to 10
Rules 11 to 18
Rules 11 to 19
Rule 19 only
questions.explanation: Section II is Rules 11 to 18: application, sailing vessels, overtaking, head-on, crossing, give-way, stand-on and responsibilities between vessels. Rules 4 to 10 are Section I. Rule 19 is Section III on its own, so 'Rules 11 to 19' wrongly mixes two sections.

questions.stem: When are two vessels 'in sight of one another' for the purposes of the Rules?
options: When each appears on the other's radar
When each receives the other's AIS signal
When one can be observed visually from the other
When they are within 2 nautical miles of each other
questions.explanation: The definition is visual: one vessel can be observed visually from the other. Radar and AIS detection do not count, however clear the picture. The Rules set no distance for being in sight.

questions.stem: In thick fog, your radar shows a vessel on your starboard bow with a steady bearing. You cannot see her. Which statement is correct?
options: You are the give-way vessel under the crossing rule, because she is on your starboard side
She is the give-way vessel, because she has you on her port side
There is no give-way or stand-on vessel between you; Rule 19 governs your actions
Neither Section II nor Section III applies until she sounds a fog signal
questions.explanation: Section II needs the vessels to be in sight of one another, so the crossing rule does not apply to a radar-only contact. In or near restricted visibility Rule 19 applies, and both vessels must act on it. Rule 19 does not wait for a fog signal; radar detection alone can call for action.

questions.stem: You are in a crossing situation with a vessel in plain sight. Which of these rules still applies to you alongside Section II?
options: None; once Section II applies, Section I is suspended
Rules 5 and 6, since Section I always applies
Rule 19, in all visibilities
Only Rule 17, because Section II overrides everything else
questions.explanation: Section I (Rules 4 to 10) applies in any condition of visibility, so lookout, safe speed, risk of collision and Rule 8 keep applying with Section II. Rule 19 only applies to vessels not in sight of one another in or near restricted visibility.

questions.stem: You are on watch in a power-driven vessel. In patchy haze you have been tracking a radar contact closing from your port bow. At 1.5 miles she comes out of the haze and you can see her clearly: a power-driven vessel crossing. What changes at the moment you see her?
options: Nothing; once you start under Rule 19 you must finish the encounter under Rule 19
Section II now applies; the crossing rule decides
You become the stand-on vessel automatically because you detected her first
Section I stops applying
questions.explanation: Rule 11 applies Section II whenever vessels are in sight of one another. Once you can see her, the crossing rule (Rule 15) sets the roles: here she has you on her starboard side, so she should keep out of the way. Who detected whom first is irrelevant, and Section I continues to apply.
